result.summary: Jove wakes on Ida, threatens Juno, and sends Iris and Apollo to make Neptune quit the field and to revive Hector. Apollo shakes the aegis and tramples the Greek wall, and the Trojans reach the ships, where Ajax defends them and Hector seizes a stern and calls for fire.

scenes.title: Jove wakes and rebukes Juno
scenes.summary: Jove wakes on Ida and sees Hector hurt and the Trojans routed. He threatens Juno, accepts her oath, and outlines the coming course of the war.
scenes.stakes: Juno risks Jove's punishment for tricking him; Hector lies wounded and the Trojan cause is failing.

scenes.title: Juno stirs the gods on Olympus
scenes.summary: Juno returns to Olympus and rouses the gods with news of Jove's wrath. Mars arms to avenge Ascalaphus, but Minerva disarms him, and Juno sends Apollo and Iris to Jove.
scenes.stakes: The gods fear Jove's punishment, and Mars risks being struck by lightning if he enters the fight.

scenes.title: Iris warns Neptune
scenes.summary: Jove sends Iris to order Neptune out of the battle. Neptune protests, citing the three-way division of the world among the brothers, then yields with a warning.
scenes.stakes: Neptune risks open conflict with Jove, who is stronger and older.

scenes.title: Apollo revives Hector
scenes.summary: Jove commands Apollo to rouse Hector and terrify the Achaeans. Apollo heals Hector, who rushes back to battle.
scenes.stakes: Hector, who thought he would die, could still be lost; the Trojans face defeat without him.

scenes.title: Apollo breaks the wall
scenes.summary: Thoas advises a rearguard stand. Apollo shakes the aegis, routs the Achaeans and tramples the trench and wall flat. Nestor prays, Jove thunders, and the Trojans pour in.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean ships and their only protection are at risk of being overrun.

scenes.title: Patroclus leaves Eurypylus
scenes.summary: Patroclus sees the breach in the wall and leaves Eurypylus to try to persuade Achilles to fight.
scenes.stakes: Achaeans may be destroyed unless Achilles can be persuaded to return to battle.

scenes.title: Fighting at the ships
scenes.summary: Ajax and Hector clash, Teucer's bowstring is broken by Jove, and many warriors fall on both sides. Jove urges Hector on, and Antilochus flees after killing Melanippus.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans risk losing their ships, and Hector is close to burning them.

scenes.title: Hector seizes a ship
scenes.summary: Nestor rallies the Achaeans and Minerva clears the darkness from their eyes. Ajax strides the decks with a sea-pike, and Hector grasps a ship's stern and calls for fire.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans' ships and return home are at stake; Ajax is nearly overwhelmed.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo, used with his name.
Danaans, Argives and Achaeans all name the Greeks.

notable_quotes.reason: Hector's declaration that dying for one's country is honourable, a famous patriotic sentiment.
Memorable simile of Apollo kicking down the wall like a child's sandcastle.
Neptune states the three-way division of the cosmos among the brothers.

analysis.text: Jove's will governs the battle, and his sketch of Patroclus's and Hector's deaths shows fate unfolding through Thetis's request. Human courage fills the space within that frame.
Quarrels among the gods mirror those among humans: Juno's deceit, Neptune's pride and Mars's grief show divine power limited by Jove's authority.

legacy.text: Hector's line that it is honourable to die fighting for one's country echoes later patriotic sentiment, notably Horace's Latin line 'dulce et decorum est pro patria mori'.

fun_facts.text: The Greek text has Apollo flatten the wall as a child kicks sand; the wall was built in Book 7 without sacrifices, and Poseidon later complains about it.

language_notes.text: "Pell-mell" means in headlong disorder, with no order or restraint.
"In half a mind" means strongly inclined; "scurvy knavery" means contemptible, base trickery.
Refers to an earlier episode in which Jove punished Juno by hanging her from the sky, as told in this speech.
Hercules, Jove's son, was driven by storms to Cos after Juno's scheming; Jove brought him back to Argos. "Suborning" means bribing or inciting.
The oath by the river Styx was the gods' most binding oath, which even Jove could not lightly break.
Recalls Thetis' plea in Book 1 that Jove honour her son Achilles by letting the Achaeans suffer; Jove's nod sealed the promise.
Holding out cups was a formal welcome, offering her a drink as a host's greeting to an arriving guest.
"Son of Saturn" is Jove; Saturn (the Greek Cronus) was the Titan father he overthrew.
"Has had a taste of them" means Mars has already suffered Jove's chosen misfortune, the death of his son.
Smiting the thighs is a conventional Homeric gesture of grief or fury.
The horses' names Panic and Rout (Greek Phobos and Deimos) personify the terrors of battle.
"Ears that hear not" echoes a proverbial charge of stubborn deafness to warning.
Ida is the mountain near Troy; Gargarus is its highest peak. 'Diadem' means a royal headband or crown.
Boreas is the north wind, personified as a god; his blasts bring cold, hail and snow.
'Great heavens!' is the translator's exclamation of indignation; 'more than he can do' means his threat exceeds what he can actually carry out.
Hades is the god of the underworld, and Rhea and Saturn are the Titan parents of the three brothers. Jove is the Greek Zeus, Neptune the Greek Poseidon.
Casting lots to divide the cosmos is an earlier mythic event; the sea, underworld and sky were allotted, while earth and Olympus stayed shared.
The Erinyes (Furies) were avenging spirits who punished wrongs, especially against elders and kin; Iris warns that Neptune's defiance of his elder brother would be punished.
'Ilius' is Ilium, Troy. 'Driver of the spoil' is an epithet for Minerva; 'Achaeans' are the Greeks.
"Holds the earth in his embrace" is a stock epithet for Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), god of the sea and earthquakes.
The gods "below with Saturn" are the Titans, imprisoned in Tartarus after Jove overthrew them; a divine quarrel might have reached them.
The aegis is Jove's storm-shield, tasselled and terrifying. Shaking it spreads panic among those it is turned against.
"Far-Darter" is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god whose arrows shoot from afar.
The "house of Hades" means the underworld, realm of the dead; Hector thought he was dying.
"Homed" is evidently a misprint for "horned"; the stag is the horned animal.
"In heaven's name" is the translator's idiom for an exclamation of surprise; Thoas is startled at seeing Hector up again.
"Profess to be the flower of the army" means those who claim to be the best fighters; Thoas challenges them to prove it.
The aegis is a divine shield or goatskin cloak, here fringed with tassels, that terrifies those who see it.
"Pell-mell" means in disorderly haste, without any formation.
Denial of funeral fire meant the dead had no proper burial rites; leaving a body to dogs was the worst dishonour.
The narrator suddenly addresses Apollo directly as "you" in mid-sentence.
Nestor recalls burnt offerings of thigh-bones wrapped in fat, the usual sacrifice that obliged a god to return favour.
The long pikes were naval spears kept on the decks for fighting from ships.
Smiting the thighs with the flat of the hands is a Homeric gesture of grief or dismay.
"Bate not a jot" means do not slacken in the least.
Lycophron had fled his home after a killing, so he lives as an exile under Ajax's protection, a common Homeric custom.
"Fain" means willing or eager; "evil" here means doom or ruin.
"Mettle" means courage and spirit.
"Allotment" means the portion of land a man holds.
"Not at a dance" means war is serious work, not play; Homer often contrasts dancing with fighting.
The sentence breaks off oddly ('sprang upon Lampus was son...'); the translation drops the object, which is Meges, the Achaean leader whom Dolops attacks.
Ephyra and the river Selleis are in western Greece; Phyleus received the corslet there from his host Euphetes, a guest-gift custom.
'Erewhile' means formerly, and 'upbraided' means scolded; both are archaic.
Ilius is Ilium, another name for Troy.
Thetis, Achilles' mother, asked Jove to give the Trojans success until the Achaeans honoured her son; 'unrighteous' reflects the harm it brings.
'Vouchsafe' means to grant graciously.
Hector is doomed to die at Achilles' hands (the son of Peleus); Pallas Minerva (Athena) will help bring it about.
Eurystheus was the king who set Hercules his labours; Copreus served as his messenger to Hercules.
"Imploring every man by his parents" means appealing to each man in the name of his parents, asking him to honour them by not shaming himself.
A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches, so the pike is enormous, around eighteen feet. "Sea-pike" is a long pole used in ship fighting.
Protesilaus was the first Greek killed at Troy, leaping ashore before the others. His ship never took him home, as the sentence says.
"Pointed at both ends" describes spears with a spike on the butt as well as the head, useful in close fighting.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted.
The "seven-foot bench" is the rowers' thwart, a long plank across the ship, here used as a platform.
"Mars" (the Greek Ares) is the god of war, so "servants of Mars" means warriors.

context_notes.text: Ida is the mountain near Troy where Jove watched the war; Neptune, Jove's brother, had been helping the Achaeans while Jove slept.
Sarpedon, Jove's son and a Trojan ally, is fated to die at Patroclus' hands; Jove here previews Patroclus' death.
Minerva favours the Achaeans, so Troy's fall fulfils her wishes; Ilius is another name for Troy.
Themis is the goddess of law and custom, who here acts as hostess and presides over the gods' assembly.
Ascalaphus, a son of Mars, led a Greek-allied Minyan contingent and was killed by Deiphobus in the fighting at Troy.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is goddess of wisdom and often restrains reckless gods and heroes.
Iris is the gods' messenger; Apollo here sides with Jove's plan and supports Troy.
Iris is the gods' swift messenger, often associated with the rainbow.
'Holds the world in his embrace' alludes to Neptune as god of the sea, which was thought to encircle the earth.
Neptune had been aiding the Greeks against Troy, so his withdrawal weakens their side.
Neptune had been helping the Achaeans against Jove's wishes. Jove has just threatened him, so Neptune withdrew.
The Hellespont is the strait (now the Dardanelles) near Troy, by which the Achaean ships lie.
Mount Ida, near Troy, is where Jove sat watching the battle.
Ajax, the huge Achaean champion, had felled Hector with a boulder earlier in this book's fighting.
Thoas leads the Aetolians from central Greece. He is respected both as a fighter and as a counsellor.
Hector had been struck down earlier by Ajax's stone and then revived by Apollo's help.
Phoebus is a title of Apollo, a god who sides with the Trojans in the Iliad.
Nestor is the oldest Greek leader, known for wisdom and long experience. Gerene is his home region.
Patroclus is Achilles' closest friend. Achilles is sitting out the war, angry at Agamemnon. This errand leads to Patroclus' fatal return in Achilles' armour.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) was patron of crafts, so skilled workmen are said to be taught by her.
Phoebus Apollo was the god of archery. Teucer, Ajax's half-brother, is the Achaeans' best archer.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, like Argives and Achaeans.
Apollo, god of prophecy and archery, favours the Trojans and often protects their warriors in battle.
The Achaean ships are drawn up on the shore; defending them means defending the Achaeans' only way home.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war, often shown as frenzied and bloodthirsty.
Homeric shields were huge, often reaching from neck to ankle, so a shield rim could trip a warrior who turned to flee.
Nestor, old king of Pylos, is the Achaeans' wise elder, often rallying them with speeches. "Gerene" is a epithet-like title tied to his homeland.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is goddess of wisdom and war, and a steady supporter of the Achaeans.
Hector refers to earlier occasions when the elders restrained him from attacking the ships. Jove (the Greek Zeus) now favours the Trojans.

literary_notes.text: "Sire of gods and men" stresses Jove's supreme authority just as he turns to rebuke Juno.
Juno piles up solemn oaths while blaming Neptune, though she has just deceived Jove; her protest sounds suspiciously excessive.
Jove outlines the deaths of Patroclus, Sarpedon and Hector in advance, giving the audience the plot's course.
Juno's speed is compared to a traveler's thought leaping across distant lands, stressing how instantly she crosses the sky.
Smiling lips against a furrowed brow show Juno's divided, resentful nature and her pretended calm.
Juno calls the gods fools for resisting Jove, though she herself repeatedly schemes against him.
Minerva's warning of Jove's punishment anticipates his dominance and the coming turn of the battle.
Jove presents himself as supreme and resents his brother's claim to equality, revealing his pride.
Iris's swift descent is compared to hail or snow driven by the north wind, conveying speed and chill.
Neptune's sneer at Jove's bragging is itself boastful, and he is about to obey the 'bragger' anyway.
The mention of the Erinyes hints at the divine penalty for defying an elder and prompts Neptune's retreat.
Apollo's swift descent is compared to a falcon, a predator of doves, foreshadowing the terror he will bring to the Achaeans.
Hector's surge is likened to a freed stallion, conveying joyful, unstoppable vigor after his weakness.
The Achaeans are like hunters who lose heart when a lion appears; Hector is the lion, a reversal of the chase.
Hearts falling into feet vividly conveys sudden, paralysing fear.
Predators attacking unguarded cattle compare the Danaans' helplessness to defenceless herds, stressing that no one protects them without Achilles or the gods.
Apollo knocking down the wall like a child's sandcastle shows how easily a god destroys human work.
The narrator turns to address Apollo directly, adding intensity and reverence to the god's act.
"All-counselling" Jove recalls his supreme wisdom and control over the war's course.
The Trojans surge over the wall like a wave over a ship's side, conveying overwhelming force.
The even carpenter's line stands for the balanced fight, with neither side gaining an advantage.
Jove breaks the bowstring, showing the gods steer the battle and protect Hector until his fated hour.
Hector's speech shows him as a patriot who values honourable death and the safety of his family.
Antilochus is compared to a dog pouncing on a wounded fawn, making his attack seem swift and predatory.
The narrator suddenly addresses the dead Melanippus directly, adding pathos to his fall.
Antilochus fleeing is likened to a guilty beast escaping a mob, which suggests fear of the crowd's retaliation.
Hector's fury is compared to Mars and a forest fire, stressing his destructive, god-driven rage.
The mention of Hector's doom by Achilles hints at his death, tempering his present victory with tragedy.
The Achaean ranks are likened to a tower and a sea cliff, conveying their unbreakable resistance.
The wave overwhelming a ship stands for Hector's assault, and the sailors' fear mirrors the Achaeans' despair.
Ajax leaping from deck to deck is compared to a circus-like horseman switching among four galloping horses, which conveys his skill, balance and the public wonder he inspires.
Hector's rush at the ship is likened to an eagle falling on a flock of birds, making the Achaeans seem helpless prey.
The ship that carried Protesilaus to Troy but not home underlines the fate of Greek heroes and the threat that this ship may now be burned.
Ajax's blunt appeal to the strength of their own hands shows him as practical, stubborn and resolute under pressure.
